scope: Task-based editorial defaults for new applications. The primary picks are reasoned editorial judgments from documented roles, not measured winners or a universal ranking. A use case identifies a strong starting profile for the stated job; it is not compatibility proof or authority to replace an existing stack.
evidence_limits: Recommendations summarize documented framework roles and primary documentation. They do not establish application fit, dependency compatibility, capacity, migration safety, production readiness, or executed setup. Apply hard constraints first and qualify the actual project.

use_cases.label: Content-led site
use_cases.why: Astro is a focused default when the main job is publishing content as mostly static pages and the product does not need an application server for each visitor.
use_cases.tradeoff: Interactive islands and server endpoints add explicit client/runtime choices; a mostly static content site should not inherit a full application backend without a requirement.

use_cases.label: Integrated web product
use_cases.why: Rails is a strong default for ordinary database-backed product work where server-rendered pages, forms, accounts, persistence and background jobs benefit from one cohesive application.
use_cases.tradeoff: It owns a running server and conventional server-rendered workflow; a client-heavy interface, a Python-centered team or a deliberate React full stack can justify another profile.

use_cases.label: Live multiuser web application
use_cases.why: Phoenix and LiveView are a strong default when multiple connected users need server-owned live interface state and the product benefits from the Elixir process and PubSub model.
use_cases.tradeoff: Persistent connections, state ownership, authorization, reconnects, fanout, overload and deployment need deliberate design and workload qualification; this recommendation does not claim a capacity limit.

use_cases.label: Python-centered data or admin web application
use_cases.why: Django is a strong default when relational data, forms, accounts, staff administration and conventional CRUD workflows are central, and the team's Python skills or ecosystem are a material product need.
use_cases.tradeoff: A rich browser-owned interface or specialized API may need a separate client or a different profile; Django's admin is a staff tool, not a substitute for product authorization and domain UI.

use_cases.label: Browser client for an existing or separate API
use_cases.why: React with Vite is a strong default when the browser UI is the deliverable and an existing or separately owned API already handles identity, permissions, data and durable work.
use_cases.tradeoff: The profile is a frontend, not a backend. Routing, server state, authentication integration and offline synchronization remain separate choices and contracts.

sources.title: React: Start a New React Project

use_cases.label: Full-stack React application
use_cases.why: Next.js is a strong default when the team deliberately wants React with server rendering, server/client components, route handlers and application logic in one web framework.
use_cases.tradeoff: The server/client boundary, caching, deployment adapter and data access need explicit design; choose it for those responsibilities rather than assuming every React app needs a full-stack framework.

use_cases.label: General-purpose HTTP API or service
use_cases.why: Go is a strong default for a standalone HTTP API or service when a small, explicit service boundary and straightforward binary deployment fit the team and operations model.
use_cases.tradeoff: Authentication, permissions, persistence conventions, administration and durable jobs require deliberate assembly; a product framework or Python integration ecosystem may reduce unrelated work.

use_cases.label: Python API for integrations or data work
use_cases.why: FastAPI is a strong default for a typed Python API when provider SDKs, data libraries or Python application code are important and automatic OpenAPI-based interface documentation helps.
use_cases.tradeoff: Identity, authorization, migrations, persistence and durable background execution are separate integrations; an ordinary data-heavy product may fit Django better.

use_cases.label: Distributed command-line tool
use_cases.why: Go is a strong default for a command-line product that should ship as a compiled binary across supported operating systems and architectures.
use_cases.tradeoff: Cross-compilation, platform behavior, packaging, terminal interaction and release signing still need target-specific verification; choose a script-oriented profile for bounded automation instead.

use_cases.label: Automation, integration or worker
use_cases.why: Python is a strong default for scheduled scripts, provider integrations, data transformations and workers when its SDK and data ecosystem directly serve the task.
use_cases.tradeoff: Persistent work needs an operated worker or workflow platform, bounded retries and idempotent external effects; a one-off script should stay small.

use_cases.label: One application for iOS and Android
use_cases.why: Expo with React Native is a strong default when one shared application team and codebase must deliver iOS and Android clients, and required native capabilities fit the Expo workflow.
use_cases.tradeoff: Native module compatibility, app lifecycle, platform-specific behavior, signing and store release still need iOS and Android qualification; use separate native profiles when platform APIs or experience dominate.

sources.title: React Native: Get started with a framework

use_cases.label: Platform-first iOS application
use_cases.why: Swift and SwiftUI are a strong default when iOS platform APIs, native interaction, accessibility, lifecycle or Apple ecosystem integration define the client.
use_cases.tradeoff: A separate Android client is needed for Android; builds and distribution require Xcode and Apple platform ownership.

use_cases.label: Platform-first Android application
use_cases.why: Kotlin and Jetpack Compose are a strong default when Android platform behavior, lifecycle, device APIs or Android-specific UX define the client.
use_cases.tradeoff: A separate iOS client is needed for iOS; device diversity, background limits, signing and release qualification remain Android-specific.

alternatives.label: Hugo content site
alternatives.choose_when: The site is a conventional static publication and the team specifically values Hugo's content organization and build model.
alternatives.caveat: This is a conditional research lead without a curated Stack Menu profile; assess templates, content authoring and deployment for the actual site.

alternatives.label: Plain HTML and CSS
alternatives.choose_when: The site is small, rarely updated and has no need for a content workflow, component system or application behavior.
alternatives.caveat: A manual page collection becomes harder to maintain as content, shared layouts or publishing needs grow.

alternatives.label: Full web application framework
alternatives.choose_when: The site also needs accounts, database-backed workflows, staff operations or durable jobs that make it an application rather than primarily published content.
alternatives.caveat: This adds an application server and product responsibilities; do not choose it solely to render mostly static content.

alternatives.label: Python product application
alternatives.choose_when: Python ecosystem integration, relational workflows, forms or built-in staff administration are central.
alternatives.caveat: Django is a product framework choice, not an automatic alternative based only on language familiarity.

alternatives.label: PHP product application
alternatives.choose_when: The team or existing system is PHP/Laravel-centered and the integrated Livewire/auth/queue conventions fit.
alternatives.caveat: The web process, queue workers and scheduler have separate operating needs; browser/client-heavy work may need a distinct client.

alternatives.label: Integrated server-rendered product application
alternatives.choose_when: A conventional integrated product matters more than Python-native data tooling or Django's administration workflow.
alternatives.caveat: This is not the same as adopting Django's built-in admin; design product-facing authorization and workflows explicitly.

alternatives.label: Full-stack React application
alternatives.choose_when: The interface is intentionally React-led and the team wants route handlers and server/client React composition in the same framework.
alternatives.caveat: It has more server/client, cache and deployment choices than a conventional integrated CRUD workflow.

alternatives.label: Separate browser client and API
alternatives.choose_when: An API already owns identity, permissions and data, or the product has a clear independent frontend/backend boundary.
alternatives.caveat: React + Vite is frontend-only and does not replace backend responsibilities.

sources.title: React: Start a New React Project

alternatives.label: Live connected web application
alternatives.choose_when: Connected multiuser state, realtime interaction or Elixir/OTP operational fit is central.
alternatives.caveat: Qualify authorization, reconnects, fanout, persistence and overload with representative workload; no capacity is implied.

alternatives.label: Integrated server-rendered application
alternatives.choose_when: The collaboration is primarily CRUD/workflow and ordinary server interactions are sufficient; live updates are a smaller feature rather than the product's central behavior.
alternatives.caveat: Reassess if shared live state, frequent presence or high fanout is central.

alternatives.label: Separate Go service
alternatives.choose_when: A separate service boundary, binary deployment, infrastructure integration or an independently scaled API is an explicit requirement.
alternatives.caveat: It is not a browser UI or full product framework; auth, persistence, jobs and client ownership must be assembled.

alternatives.label: Rust HTTP service
alternatives.choose_when: A measured resource or latency constraint, an existing Rust service boundary, or a required Rust library justifies the language and asynchronous service model.
alternatives.caveat: The curated Rust service guide starts with Cargo and treats Axum, Tokio and database integrations as explicit composition choices. Measure the reason to accept their runtime and type complexity.

alternatives.label: TypeScript API on Cloudflare Workers
alternatives.choose_when: The API is intentionally deployed to Cloudflare Workers and the team wants a Web Standards-based TypeScript routing layer.
alternatives.caveat: Runtime APIs, storage, background work and limits are provider-specific; there is no curated Stack Menu profile for this deployment.

alternatives.label: Python API and data application
alternatives.choose_when: The API is closely tied to relational product data, forms, staff administration or conventional Django workflows.
alternatives.caveat: Django's product framework can be broader than a narrow stateless service needs.

alternatives.label: Python API framework
alternatives.choose_when: The service specifically benefits from Python integrations, typed request/response models or OpenAPI generation.
alternatives.caveat: Choose Go for a general standalone API when Python's ecosystem is not a material need; FastAPI still needs explicit auth, persistence and jobs.

alternatives.label: Rust command-line product
alternatives.choose_when: A Rust library or measured resource-control requirement materially benefits the product and the team can own Rust tooling and target verification.
alternatives.caveat: Rust adds language, tooling and cross-compilation complexity; use Go for conventional compiled distribution when those constraints do not matter. An asynchronous runtime is an additional choice only when the workload needs it.

alternatives.label: Full-stack Svelte application
alternatives.choose_when: The team has a concrete Svelte/SvelteKit ecosystem preference and wants its routing and server/client application model.
alternatives.caveat: There is no curated Stack Menu profile here; validate the current adapter, rendering and server boundary before choosing it.

alternatives.label: Full-stack Vue application
alternatives.choose_when: The project or team is materially invested in Vue/Nuxt and wants an integrated full-stack application framework.
alternatives.caveat: There is no curated Stack Menu profile here; validate the current Nuxt version, modules, deployment adapter and server/client boundary.

alternatives.label: Separate native iOS and Android clients
alternatives.choose_when: Platform-first experience, native APIs, lifecycle behavior or platform distribution justify separate teams/codebases for iOS and Android.
alternatives.caveat: This changes the one-shared-codebase premise: it is a two-client composition with two delivery and verification paths.

alternatives.label: Flutter iOS and Android application
alternatives.choose_when: A shared Dart and Flutter application fits the team's skills, UI needs and required native platform capabilities.
alternatives.caveat: There is no curated Stack Menu Flutter profile; verify plugin support, platform behavior, tooling and release paths for both targets.

alternatives.label: Typed React routing and server functions
alternatives.choose_when: Only when type-safe file-based routing or framework-provided server functions directly solve a stated requirement and the project owner wants a JavaScript/TypeScript alternative.
alternatives.caveat: TanStack Start 1.0 is stable, but there is no curated Stack Menu profile. Check its runtime adapters, server boundary and documentation for the chosen version; it is a conditional research lead, not a default or a reason to migrate a healthy application.
